quote: Paul Ekman (a pioneer in the study of tiny facial muscle movements) could probably read off a sizeable fraction of the world’s lies right now, given a chance.
content: This one is conceded. Bond & DePaulo had settled it, and the Ekman sentence should go. The essay's thesis is the entanglement of facts, and the entanglement of facts is where lie detection turned out to work. In the Strategic Use of Evidence technique, interviewers hold back what they know and check the suspect's story against it, the way the essay's spouse checks the "business trip." Trained interviewers reached about 85% accuracy against 56% for untrained ones (Hartwig et al. 2006). The web could not be read off a face, and it could be read off the story. Faces carry little information about deception, and the essay's dialogue shows the channel that does.

quote: But the Great Web is very commonly underestimated.
content: The diary studies report lies as seen by the liar, who cannot know which lies were quietly seen through. When researchers asked people how they had actually discovered lies told to them, the answers were mostly third-party information and physical evidence, often uncovered weeks or months later, and rarely demeanour at the time (Park et al. 2002). That is the essay's mechanism: the lie is caught through an entangled fact the liar did not control. The essay's examples of engineered detection have also multiplied. Relatives' DNA uploaded to genealogy databases could already identify most Americans of European descent by 2018 (Erlich et al. 2018), and that is how decades-old cases such as the Golden State Killer were solved. The web was underestimated even by those who knew it was there.

quote: A student of evolutionary biology can see the design signature of natural selection on every wolf that chases a rabbit; and every rabbit that runs away; and every bee that stings instead of broadcasting a polite warning—but the deceptions of creationists sound plausible to them, I’m sure.
content: The sentence names two populations: the "deceptions of creationists," and the people to whom they "sound plausible." Evans's default teleology explains why the second group finds them plausible. The first group exists and wrote down its strategy. The Discovery Institute's "Wedge" document (1998) set out a public-relations plan to replace "materialist" science with design, beginning with "the thin edge of the wedge" in schools. The contagion the essay describes starts there. A sincere folk theory needs no cover-up until it is defended against biology. Once it is, the defence has to misrepresent the fossil record, the meaning of "theory," and the rules of evidence, and those misrepresentations are what the untrained default finds plausible.
